definition: Computational photography refers to digital image capture and processing techniques that use digital computation instead of optical processes.
details: Computational photography can improve the capabilities of a camera, or introduce features that were not possible at all with film-based photography, or reduce the cost or size of camera elements. Examples of computational photography include in-camera computation of digital panoramas, high-dynamic-range images, and light field cameras. Light field cameras use novel optical elements to capture three-dimensional scene information, which can then be used to produce 3D images, enhanced depth-of-field, and selective de-focusing (or "post focus"). Enhanced depth-of-field reduces the need for mechanical focusing systems. All of these features use computational imaging techniques. The definition of computational photography has evolved to cover a number of subject areas in computer graphics, computer vision, and applied optics. These areas are given below, organized according to a taxonomy proposed by Shree K. Nayar. Within each area is a list of techniques, and for each technique, one or two representative papers or books are cited. Deliberately omitted from the taxonomy are image processing (see also digital image processing) techniques applied to traditionally captured images to produce

explainer.lead: Computational photography uses digital processing to do jobs that would otherwise require optics, or to create images that film photography could not produce. It can add capabilities such as post-capture refocusing while also reducing a camera's cost, size, or reliance on mechanical focusing.

tiers.eli5: Think of a camera as both an eye and a brain: the eye gathers light, and the brain helps decide what the finished picture should look like. That brain can stitch together a panorama, make a high-dynamic-range image, or use extra scene information to change which part looks sharp after the picture is taken.
tiers.practitioner: Apply it when capture and computation are designed together, as with in-camera panoramas, high-dynamic-range images, or light-field cameras. Light-field systems pair novel optical elements with processing of three-dimensional scene information to produce 3D images, enhanced depth of field, and selective defocusing. A key distinction is that Nayar's taxonomy deliberately leaves out ordinary image processing applied to traditionally captured images.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational photography = digital image capture and processing in which digital computation replaces optical processes. Its scope spans computer graphics, computer vision, and applied optics, with Shree K. Nayar's taxonomy organizing the subject areas and techniques. Representative techniques include in-camera panoramas, high-dynamic-range imaging, and light-field capture for 3D images, enhanced depth of field, and post focus. Enhanced depth of field can reduce the need for mechanical focusing systems.

explainer.example: A light-field camera uses novel optical elements to capture three-dimensional scene information. Computation then uses that information to selectively defocus parts of the image after capture, providing a 'post focus' capability.

explainer.intuition: Instead of asking lenses and mechanical systems to determine every aspect of the final image, capture useful scene data and let computation finish the job. This shifts part of image formation from optics into digital processing.
howItWorks: Capture the scene as digital image data.
Optionally use novel optical elements to record three-dimensional scene information.
Process the captured data with computational imaging techniques.
Produce outputs such as panoramas, high-dynamic-range images, 3D images, or selective defocusing.
explainer.whyItMatters: It can extend what a camera can do, introduce features impossible with film-based photography, and reduce the cost or size of camera elements. Enhanced depth of field can also reduce the need for mechanical focusing systems.
misconceptions: It does not eliminate optics entirely; light-field cameras still use novel optical elements.
Under Nayar's taxonomy, it is not simply ordinary image processing applied to traditionally captured images.
